title: Highest-Fiber Foods: Ranking per 100 Grams and by Serving

seo.title: Highest-Fiber Foods: Ranking and Servings
seo.meta_description: Compare chia, flax, legumes, nuts, fruit and vegetables by fiber per 100 grams and by realistic serving size.
seo.search_intent: Find high-fiber foods and understand concentration versus serving size.

excerpt: Chia and flax lead on fiber per 100 grams, while a full serving of beans or lentils can contribute more total fiber than a spoonful of seeds.
content_html:
Fiber is found almost entirely in plant foods, but the concentration varies enormously. Dry seeds lead per 100 grams, legumes become especially impressive by the bowl, and fruits and vegetables contribute fiber along with a large amount of water.

Fiber ranking per 100 grams

FoodApprox. fiber
Chia seeds34 g
Flaxseed27 g
Almonds12.5 g
Dry oats~10 g
Cooked lentils~7.9 g
Cooked chickpeas~7.6 g
Avocado6.7 g
Raspberries6.5 g
Cooked green peas~5.5 g
Cooked artichoke~5.4 g
Pear with skin~3.1 g
Cooked broccoli~3.3 g

Chia and flax: concentrated in a small serving

Chia provides about 34 g/100 g and flax about 27 g/100 g. A 20 g portion of chia supplies roughly 6.8 g fiber; the same amount of flax supplies about 5.4 g.

Legumes: a full serving changes the ranking

Cooked lentils contain roughly 7.9 g fiber per 100 g and chickpeas around 7.6 g. A 1-cup serving near 200 g can provide roughly 15–16 g fiber, more than a normal sprinkle of seeds.

Legumes also bring protein, folate, potassium, nonheme iron and carbohydrate, which is why they can have a large effect on the fiber content of an entire meal.

Almonds and oats

Almonds are about 12.5 g fiber per 100 g; a 1-ounce / 28 g handful supplies roughly 3.5 g. Dry oats are near 10 g/100 g, so a 50 g portion supplies about 5 g.

Cooking oats with water or milk increases the weight of the bowl without creating or removing much fiber, so the value per 100 g of prepared oatmeal is lower than the dry value.

High-fiber fruit

Raspberries and avocado contain roughly 6.5–6.7 g fiber per 100 g, about twice the 3.1 g/100 g in a pear with skin. A 125 g serving of raspberries provides about 8 g fiber.

Avocado is unusual because it also contains substantial fat. It provides about 160 calories/100 g versus roughly 52 calories/100 g for raspberries.

Vegetables

Artichokes, peas and broccoli have less fiber per 100 g than dry seeds, but their usual portions are larger. One medium artichoke can provide around 7 g fiber; 150 g cooked broccoli provides around 5 g.

How much fiber should adults get?

The FDA Daily Value is 28 g fiber per day on a 2,000-calorie diet. Individual calorie needs vary, but the number gives useful context for food labels.

A simple way to reach the Daily Value

FoodServingApprox. fiber
Oats50 g5 g
Raspberries125 g8 g
Cooked lentils150 g12 g
Almonds1 oz3.5 g

Those foods alone total about 28–29 g before counting vegetables, bread or other fruit.

Different types of fiber

Fiber is not one compound. Oats and legumes contain important soluble and fermentable fractions; whole grains, vegetables, seeds and fruit contain varying mixtures of soluble and insoluble fibers. Variety helps provide a broader mix.

Increase fiber gradually

A sudden jump from a low-fiber diet to large portions of beans, bran and seeds can cause gas or bloating. Gradual increases and normal fluid intake are often easier to tolerate.

Bottom line

Chia and flax lead by concentration, legumes shine by serving size, and fruits and vegetables add fiber with water and volume. The strongest pattern uses several food groups rather than one fiber champion.

Sources

Food values come from USDA FoodData Central. The 28 g Daily Value comes from FDA nutrition-label guidance.

faq.question: What food is highest in fiber?
faq.answer: Chia and flax are among the most concentrated common foods, at about 34 and 27 g per 100 g.

faq.question: How much fiber is in lentils?
faq.answer: Cooked lentils are roughly 7.9 g/100 g, so a 200 g serving can provide about 16 g.

faq.question: What is the U.S. Daily Value for fiber?
faq.answer: The FDA Daily Value is 28 g per day on a 2,000-calorie diet.
